topic: The Logic of Light: Proving Snell's Law via Fermat's Principle
target_audience: First-year University Physics Students or Advanced High School Students

outline.topic: The Logic of Light: Proving Snell's Law via Fermat's Principle
outline.target_audience: First-year University Physics Students or Advanced High School Students

sections.title: The Lifeguard's Dilemma (Introduction)
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'Least Time' using a relatable analogy. Explain that the fastest path between two points in different media is not always a straight line if the speeds in those media differ.
sections.example: An animation of a lifeguard on a beach needing to reach a swimmer in the ocean. The lifeguard runs faster on sand than they swim in water. A split-screen compares a straight-line path versus a 'bent' path that maximizes time on the sand, showing the 'bent' path arrives first.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Light Speed and Refractive Index
sections.content: Define the relationship between the speed of light in a vacuum (c), the speed in a medium (v), and the refractive index (n). Establish the formula v = c/n.
sections.example: A visual chart showing light slowing down as it moves from air (n≈1) to glass (n≈1.5), represented by a changing velocity vector arrow and shifting color/wavelength.

sections.title: Setting the Stage: The Geometry of Refraction
sections.content: Construct a coordinate system for a light ray traveling from Point A (medium 1) to Point B (medium 2). Define the horizontal distance 'L', the vertical heights 'h1' and 'h2', and the variable point 'x' where light hits the interface.
sections.example: A clear geometric diagram showing a ray crossing a horizontal boundary. Use labels: h1 (vertical distance to A), h2 (vertical distance to B), x (distance from A's projection to the hit point), and L-x (remaining distance to B's projection).

sections.title: The Principle of Least Time (Fermat's Principle)
sections.content: State Fermat's Principle: Light follows the path that takes the least time. Express total time (T) as the sum of travel times in both media: T = (Path Length 1 / v1) + (Path Length 2 / v2).
sections.example: An equation block appearing alongside the diagram: T(x) = [sqrt(h1² + x²) / v1] + [sqrt(h2² + (L-x)²) / v2]. Highlight how T depends on the position of x.

sections.title: Calculus and the Optimization Step
sections.content: To find the minimum time, take the derivative of T with respect to x and set it to zero (dT/dx = 0). Show the differentiation process and how the terms relate to the geometry of the angles.
sections.example: Animated math steps showing: x / (v1 * sqrt(h1² + x²)) = (L-x) / (v2 * sqrt(h2² + (L-x)²)). Overlay the diagram to show that x/hypotenuse is sin(θ1) and (L-x)/hypotenuse is sin(θ2).

sections.title: The Final Derivation: Snell's Law
sections.content: Substitute the sine terms into the derived equation: sin(θ1)/v1 = sin(θ2)/v2. Then, replace velocities with refractive indices (v = c/n) to reach the final form: n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2).
sections.example: A glowing transition where the fraction sin(θ1)/(c/n1) = sin(θ2)/(c/n2) simplifies and rearranges into the iconic n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2) inside a golden frame.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Disappearing Straw
sections.content: Briefly conclude by applying the law to a common observation to reinforce the concept of optical bending.
sections.example: A 3D render of a straw in a glass of water. Use Snell's Law to calculate the 'apparent' position of the straw vs. its 'actual' position, showing why the straw looks broken at the water's surface.

storyboard.title: The Lifeguard's Dilemma (Introduction)
lecture_lines: To save a swimmer, a lifeguard must move fast.
Running is faster than swimming across the water.
The quickest path is not a straight line.
animations: Show beach (top, #C2B280) and water (bottom, #0000FF) with lifeguard A and swimmer B.
A dot moves slowly along a straight path (#888888) from lifeguard to swimmer.
A second dot moves along a bent path (#FFFF00) that maximizes sand distance.
The bent path dot finishes the race ahead of the straight path dot.
Highlight the optimal bent path and label it "Least Time" in gold (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Light Speed and Refractive Index
lecture_lines: Light speed changes depending on the medium.
Refractive index n relates vacuum to medium speed.
We define velocity in a medium as v = c/n.
animations: Ray (white #FFFFFF) moves from vacuum into a glass medium.
Ray slows down inside the glass, turning cyan (#00FFFF).
Formula v = c / n appears in yellow (#FFFF00) next to the medium.

storyboard.title: Setting the Stage: The Geometry of Refraction
lecture_lines: Light travels from point A to point B.
Points A and B have heights h1 and h2.
The total horizontal distance is L.
Light hits the interface at point x.
The remaining horizontal distance is L minus x.
animations: Draw a horizontal interface (#FFFFFF) with Point A (above) and Point B (below).
Add vertical dashed lines for heights h1 and h2 from points to interface.
Show total horizontal distance L and the variable hit point x on interface.
Draw a ray from A to x, then to B, forming angles θ1 and θ2.
Label segments x and L-x on the interface in light blue (#ADD8E6).

storyboard.title: The Principle of Least Time (Fermat's Principle)
lecture_lines: Fermat's Principle: Light takes the path of least time.
Total time is the sum of travel times.
Express time T as distance divided by velocity.
animations: State "Principle of Least Time" in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
Display the total time formula T = (Path 1 / v1) + (Path 2 / v2).
Substitute lengths: T(x) = [sqrt(h1² + x²) / v1] + [sqrt(h2² + (L-x)²) / v2] in pink (#FF00FF).

storyboard.title: Calculus and the Optimization Step
lecture_lines: To minimize time, we set the derivative to zero.
Differentiate the time equation with respect to x.
The resulting terms relate to the travel angles.
Ratio x over hypotenuse equals sine of theta 1.
Ratio L minus x over hypotenuse equals sine theta 2.
animations: Display the derivative equation dT/dx = 0 in white (#FFFFFF).
Show the differentiation step resulting in a ratio equality equation.
Highlight x/hypotenuse and (L-x)/hypotenuse on the geometry diagram.
Replace the highlighted ratios with sin(θ1) and sin(θ2) labels.
Conclude with sin(θ1)/v1 = sin(θ2)/v2 in light green (#90EE90).

storyboard.title: The Final Derivation: Snell's Law
lecture_lines: Equating terms gives sin theta 1 over v1.
Substitute velocity v with c over n.
The speed of light c cancels out.
Rearrange to get n1 sin theta 1 equals n2 sin theta 2.
This is Snell's Law derived from Fermat's Principle.
animations: Show sin(θ1)/v1 = sin(θ2)/v2 in white (#FFFFFF).
Substitute v = c/n to introduce refractive indices n1 and n2.
Final Snell's Law n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2) appears in a golden box (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: Real-World Application: The Disappearing Straw
lecture_lines: A straw looks broken when placed in water.
Refraction bends light rays leaving the liquid.
Snell's Law explains this common optical illusion.
animations: Show a straight straw in a glass of water (#FFFFFF).
Draw light rays from the straw tip bending at the water surface.
The apparent straw image appears bent and highlighted in red (#FF0000).
